explain.headline: India’s Model BIT: A Decade Later, Amid Changes
static: A Bilateral Investment Treaty is an agreement between two countries to establish terms and conditions for private investments by nationals and companies of one state in another.
The Model BIT serves as a country’s opening template during treaty negotiations, outlining the standard protections offered and obligations expected from foreign investors.
Investor-State Dispute Settlement is a mechanism that allows foreign investors to sue host governments before international arbitration tribunals for treaty breaches.
The Most Favoured Nation clause requires a country to treat investors from one treaty partner no less favorably than those from any other country.
Fair and Equitable Treatment is a standard international law principle ensuring foreign investments are treated in a non-arbitrary, transparent, and due-process-abiding manner.
explain.what: The editorial discusses the proposed revision of India’s Model Bilateral Investment Treaty a decade after its 2015 introduction, evaluating how recent state practice and international reforms should shape the new template.
explain.why_in_news: The Union Budget 2025-26 announced the revamp of India’s Model Bilateral Investment Treaty, and a revised version is reportedly finalised and awaiting Cabinet approval.
explain.background: India adopted a defensive Model BIT in 2015 requiring lengthy local court litigation after adverse historical arbitration awards, but recent agreements with countries like the UAE show a shift toward greater flexibility.
significance: Crucial for shaping India's future foreign direct investment inflows while preserving state regulatory powers.
Important for understanding India's evolving stance on international arbitration and investor-state dispute settlement reforms.
Relevant for GS-2 (International Relations) and GS-3 (Economy and Investment).

texts.x: UPSC Syllabus: Gs Paper 2- Indian economy Introduction India is revising its Model Bilateral Investment Treaty (BIT) nearly a decade after adopting the 2015 framework. The review comes as India’s treaty practice and the global investment regime have changed. The key issue is not simply whether investors should receive more or less protection, but how…
India must draw lessons from a decade of investment treaty experience

points: The Union Budget 2025-26 announced that India’s Model Bilateral Investment Treaty would be revamped and made more investor-friendly.
India turned cautious on investment treaties after the 2011 White Industries award against India and worries over investor-state dispute settlement.
The 2015 Model narrowed investment definitions, kept regulatory exceptions, and required investors to exhaust local remedies for five years before arbitration.
Since 2015, India concluded newer agreements with the UAE, Uzbekistan, and Israel, cutting the local remedies period to three years.
UN Trade and Development records global treaties moving toward investment facilitation and narrower protections, relying less on investor-state dispute settlement.
The UN Commission on International Trade Law is examining a permanent tribunal with an appellate mechanism and rules on damages.
Recent Indian treaties like the UAE and Israel agreements and the India-Uzbekistan BIT departed from the rigid 2015 text by allowing counterclaims.
The revised model must address Most Favoured Nation clause scopes, precise Fair and Equitable Treatment definitions, and dispute prevention to balance investment and regulation.
sum.text:
India’s treaty practice has already moved ahead of its model. The UAE, Uzbekistan and Israel agreements shortened the remedies period and allowed counterclaims while the 2015 text stayed unchanged. The revision matters only if it writes this practice into the model. If it does not, the model remains a reference that negotiators bypass.
The Union Budget 2025-26 announced that India’s Model Bilateral Investment Treaty (BIT) would be revamped and made more investor-friendly , and the revised model is reportedly finalised and awaiting Cabinet approval . The real question is not whether investors get more or less protection, but what India has learnt from a decade of treaty practice .
What it is: A BIT protects one country’s investors in the other. A Model BIT is India’s opening template, like a standard contract form, showing the protections it offers and obligations it expects.
Why it turned cautious: The White Industries Australia Limited vs Republic of India award (2011) and worries about investor-state dispute settlement (ISDS) , where investors sue states before international tribunals, made India defensive.
Design of the 2015 Model: It narrowed what counts as an investment and kept regulatory exceptions for state action. Investors had to exhaust local remedies for five years , using Indian courts first, before arbitration.
The takeaway: After nearly a decade, the revision decides whether India keeps this defensive design or trades some of it for investor confidence.
New-generation agreements: Since 2015, India has concluded newer investment agreements with the United Arab Emirates (UAE) , Uzbekistan and Israel .
Shorter local remedies: The India-UAE BIT and the India-Israel Bilateral Investment Agreement , in force since July 2026 , cut the local remedies period to three years .
Greater flexibility: These treaties show India has already departed from its own model in practice.
UNCTAD’s shift: UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD) records treaties moving toward investment facilitation , making investing procedurally easier, with narrower protections. They rely less on ISDS.
UNCITRAL reform agenda: The UN Commission on International Trade Law (UNCITRAL) is examining a permanent tribunal with an appellate mechanism to correct errors. It is also studying rules on damages and dispute prevention.
Rule-shaper, not rule-taker: Scholar Makane Moïse Mbengue argues a developing state can shape investment law through its treaties, so India’s model must answer this new…

explain.headline: India's 2016 Model Bilateral Investment Treaty and Declining Foreign Investment
static: A Bilateral Investment Treaty protects investments made by investors of one contracting state in the territory of the other contracting state, usually providing for investor-state dispute settlement.
The 2016 Indian Model BIT was adopted to rebalance investment protection in favor of the state's right to regulate, notably excluding tax matters and mandating local exhaustion of remedies.

The OECD Benchmark Definition of Foreign Direct Investment sets international standards for compiling FDI statistics, defining it by a lasting interest and a management stake (typically 10% voting power).
Net foreign direct investment accounts for foreign direct investment inflows minus disinvestment and repatriation of capital by foreign investors.
International arbitration allows foreign investors to take sovereign states to neutral tribunals if treaty breaches occur, bypassing domestic judicial delays.
explain.what: An opinion piece discussing how India's restrictive 2016 Model Bilateral Investment Treaty has shrunk its treaty network and suppressed net foreign investment.
explain.why_in_news: Eighteen months after the Finance Minister promised Parliament a revision of the 2016 Model BIT, the model remains unchanged while net FDI touches historic lows.
explain.background: India's 2016 Model BIT introduced a mandatory five-year local litigation rule before international arbitration, making foreign capital commitments difficult and shrinking India's treaty partnerships.
significance: Highlights the widening gap between gross FDI inflows and weak net foreign capital additions in India.
Examines how rigid investor-state dispute settlement templates affect sovereign economic ties and trade negotiations.
Provides critical insights into global economic standards like the OECD definition of FDI versus domestic data modifications.

Gross FDI inflow for 2025-26 reached a record $94.5 billion.

stories.ai_why: Analysis of India's model investment treaty and bilateral trade impacts.

points: India's bilateral investment treaties in force dropped significantly from 73 in 2015 to just eight by 2021 following the strict 2016 Model BIT.
The 2016 Model BIT requires foreign investors to litigate in local courts for five years before accessing international arbitration, causing severe delays.
Global norms typically require only a three to six month consultation period to settle disputes, making India's terms extremely restrictive.
Although gross FDI inflows hit a record $94.5 billion, net FDI fell to about 0.18% of GDP, which is the second-lowest in three decades.
Foreign investors repatriated or sold off $53.6 billion while Indian firms invested $33.3 billion abroad, reflecting weak net capital commitments.
Reinvested earnings reached $25.6 billion, which exceeds three times the net FDI, showing that fresh foreign capital commitments remain subdued.
A reported proposal to count portfolio investment held over three years as direct investment deviates from the OECD Benchmark Definition of FDI.
The author argues that the Department of Economic Affairs should revise the Model BIT to replace mandatory local litigation with a short consultation window.
sum.text:
India’s bilateral investment treaties (BITs) in force fell from 73 in 2015 to eight by 2021 after the 2016 Model BIT tightened its terms for foreign investors. Eighteen months after the Finance Minister promised Parliament a revision, the model is unchanged and foreign investment stays weak.
What it is: A BIT protects one country’s investors in the other and lets them take disputes to international arbitration , a neutral tribunal. The 2016 Model is India’s negotiating template.
Five-year local litigation rule: A foreign investor must litigate in Indian courts for five years before arbitration. Indian courts rarely finish a case in that time, so the rule brought only delay .
Global norm: Other countries require only a three to six month consultation period , like a cooling-off period before a divorce, to try to settle.
Partial easing: Newer treaties with the United Arab Emirates (UAE) and Israel cut the wait to three years ; proposals for two give no stated reason.
The takeaway: The model made arbitration hard to reach, so India’s treaty network shrank.
Treaty network dismantled: The new model produced only six new treaties . None of the eight still in force covers a significant source of foreign capital.
Investment forgone: American investment is large even without a treaty; the cost is the extra investment a treaty would add.
Obstruction charge: India is described as the most obstructionist member of the World Trade Organization (WTO) , with a matching treaty model. Deregulation and a US trade deal have also stalled.
Gross versus net: Net foreign direct investment (FDI) is money coming in minus money going out. Gross inflow hit a record, but net FDI was only $7.65 billion last year.
Money going out: Foreign investors took home or sold off $53.6 billion , and Indian firms invested $33.3 billion abroad .
Reinvested earnings: Profits foreign firms reinvest in India reached $25.6 billion , over three times net FDI. This is not a fresh commitment .
Older definition: Excluding reinvested earnings, as India once did, gives a net direct investment outflow of about $18 billion .
Portfolio exit: Indian shares trail other emerging markets by about 30 percentage points this year. Foreign investors have pulled out another $10.5 billion .
What separates the two: Direct investment is a stake large enough to give a say in running the business ; portfolio investment is too small for that.

explain.headline: Needed: A Super El Niño Abhiyan to combat extreme weather threats
static: El Niño is a climate pattern characterized by the warming of surface ocean waters in the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean.
The Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) and El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) significantly influence the intensity and distribution of the Indian southwest monsoon.
Coral bleaching occurs when corals expel symbiotic algae due to elevated water temperatures, often triggered during intense marine heatwaves and El Niño events.
The Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services (INCOIS) provides ocean information and advisory services including potential fishing zone advisories and tsunami early warnings.
Climate change exacerbates the frequency and severity of extreme weather events such as unseasonal rainfall, prolonged droughts, and severe cyclones across Indian districts.
explain.what: The article warns of an upcoming severe 'Super El Niño' event projected for 2026-2027 and calls for a multi-sectoral 'Super El Niño Abhiyan' to proactively gather ecological data and build climate resilience in India.
explain.why_in_news: Global scientific institutions including the WMO and NOAA have issued high-confidence forecasts predicting a strong to very strong El Niño continuing into spring 2027.
explain.background: El Niño events warm Pacific waters, disrupting global climate systems and heavily impacting Indian monsoon rainfall, agricultural productivity, and marine ecosystems.
significance: Highlights the compounding threats of global warming and a severe El Niño on India's agriculture, water security, and rural livelihoods.
Emphasizes the urgent need to bridge critical data gaps in terrestrial and marine ecosystems through proactive scientific monitoring.
Proposes a collaborative framework between government, scientists, and philanthropic capital to generate actionable resilience strategies.
prelims: WMO and NOAA forecast a 97 per cent probability of the El Niño continuing into spring 2027.
Pacific Ocean temperatures have risen 2.6°C above the typical El Niño threshold of 0.5°C.
NCF researchers recorded a 50 per cent decline in coral reefs around Lakshadweep between 1998 and 2025.
INCOIS predicts severe heat stress on the Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal peaking around March 2027.
explain.mains: Examine the linkages between Pacific El Niño events and India's climate vulnerabilities. Discuss the necessity of a coordinated multi-sectoral approach to build long-term ecological and agrarian resilience.

stories.ai_why: Discusses preparedness and policy response to climate phenomena like El Nino.

points: Global scientific bodies like the WMO and NOAA express high confidence that a strong to very strong El Niño will continue into spring 2027.
This supersized El Niño threatens massive economic blows and could be the worst event in a millennium based on 1,000-year coral-core climate records.
The author argues that Pacific El Niño events disrupt Indian monsoon winds, historically causing severe droughts in years like 1972, 2002, and 2009.
India is already vulnerable to extreme weather, with 86 per cent of days seeing extreme events in 2023 and 85 per cent of districts exposed to climate disasters.
Pacific Ocean temperatures have risen 2.6°C above the El Niño threshold, with projections suggesting anomalies could reach up to 4°C.
Marine systems face severe risks, as INCOIS predicts heavy heat stress on the Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal peaking around March 2027, threatening fisherfolk livelihoods.
Terrestrial systems, agriculture, and pastoralists face unmapped risks, while the southwest monsoon has closed below its long-period average with thin reservoirs heading into rabi.
On September 16, 188 conservationists and researchers issued a call to ecologists for proactive, real-time data gathering and multi-sectoral cooperation.
The author proposes a Super El Niño Abhiyan combining scientific evidence, administrative readiness, and societal empathy, backed by government facilitation and philanthropic capital.
sum.text:
Very rarely, it is okay to be alarmist. This is one of those times. Even usually cautious scientists seem to agree. For the first time, the World Meteorological Organisation (WMO), the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), and other reputed global scientific research institutions have expressed a high degree of confidence in their 2026 El Niño forecast . They offer a 97 per cent probability that it will continue into spring 2027. The NOAA puts 80 per cent-plus odds on it becoming a strong to very strong event, with sea surface temperature anomalies exceeding 2°C, a threshold rarely crossed in the key Pacific monitoring region. The UN warns that this “supersized” El Niño has the potential to deliver massive blows to economies globally. Based on 1,000-year coral-core climate records, media report this could be the worst event in a millennium.
Why should we in India care about what’s happening in the Pacific Ocean? The Pacific El Niño and our Indian monsoon are inextricably tied together. The heat in the ocean drives moisture-laden winds. When the Pacific becomes unusually warm, it will disrupt the very wind systems that pull rains towards India. Often, alongside a strong El Niño, we have experienced some of our worst droughts, such as in 1972, 2002 and 2009.
This “Super El Niño” is coming on top of a long-term trend of global warming, which we have seen can exacerbate extreme weather. In India, disasters are no longer exceptional events. In 2023, for example, 86 per cent of days witnessed an extreme weather event, with more than 2.2 million hectares of cropland damaged. About 85 per cent of districts are exposed to floods, droughts, or cyclones.
This year’s El Niño might be like a new blow to an open wound.
We might have to plan for the worst. Yet, we don’t know how it will affect terrestrial systems inside the country — our grasslands, forests, or riverine systems — or impact the phenology, the growth and fruiting of plants. We do not understand how it will affect agriculturists and pastoralists, nor can we predict the exact impact on our marine systems. Pacific Ocean temperatures have already risen 2.6°C above the threshold typically used to define El Niño (0.5°C), with projections suggesting anomalies could reach up to 4°C. At such temperatures, we can expect several coral reefs to bleach and die out. explain.headline: For constituting poll body, a lesson from the UN on institutional trust
static: Article 324 of the Indian Constitution provides for the establishment of the Election Commission of India to superintend, direct, and control elections.
The Election Commission consists of the Chief Election Commissioner and such number of other Election Commissioners as the President determines from time to time.
Historically, appointments were made solely by the executive under presidential authority in the absence of a dedicated parliamentary legislation for nearly 75 years.
The 2023 Supreme Court ruling temporarily established a panel of the PM, Leader of the Opposition, and Chief Justice of India to ensure neutrality.
Parliament subsequently enacted the Chief Election Commissioner and other Election Commissioners Act, 2023, substituting the CJI with a Union Cabinet Minister.
explain.what: The editorial discusses the appointment mechanism of the Election Commission of India, arguing for a consensus-based approach inspired by the United Nations to ensure independence and public trust.
explain.why_in_news: Recent concerns regarding the functioning of election officials and a Supreme Court split verdict highlighted the debate over exclusive executive control in appointing poll panel members.
explain.background: Article 324 mandates an independent Election Commission, but successive governments appointed members without a specific parliamentary law until recent legislative and judicial interventions.
significance: Ensures the Election Commission is perceived as fair and impartial, which is vital for the survival of electoral democracy.
Reduces executive dominance in poll body appointments through bipartisan consensus and judicial representation.
Enhances public confidence by drawing comparative institutional lessons from global bodies like the UN.
prelims: Article 324 of the Indian Constitution governs the Election Commission.
The 2023 Act replaced the Chief Justice of India with a Union Cabinet Minister in the selection committee.
The Cabinet Secretary prepares the shortlist of candidates for the selection committee.
Decisions in the current selection committee are taken by a majority vote.

points: Recent controversies over the Election Commission and a Supreme Court split verdict highlight the need to protect public trust in India's electoral system.
Article 324 of the Constitution vests the superintendence and conduct of elections in the Election Commission of India comprising the CEC and other ECs.
For 75 years the executive made these appointments without a specific parliamentary law until the Supreme Court intervened in March 2023.
The Supreme Court mandated a committee of the Prime Minister, Leader of Opposition, and Chief Justice of India until Parliament enacted a law.
Parliament enacted a law in 2023 replacing the Chief Justice with a Union Cabinet Minister, giving the government a potential numerical dominance.
The author argues that drawing from the UN Secretary-General selection model can help build institutional trust and avoid political bias.
The UN Security Council veto principle shows that a candidate must be acceptable and not distrusted by major stakeholders rather than being purely technical.
Reforming the ECI appointment panel to include the Chief Justice of India and building bipartisan consensus will safeguard institutional independence and public confidence.
sum.text:
Context: Two recent developments highlight the need to protect public trust in India’s electoral system. Concerns were raised over the functioning of the CEC and senior EC officials, while a Supreme Court split verdict stressed that the executive should not have exclusive control over appointing the CEC and ECs. These developments underline the need for an independent and impartial Election Commission.
Article 324 in the Indian Constitution gives power to the Election Commission to direct, control, and conduct elections to all Parliament, to the Legislature of every state and of elections to the offices of the President and Vice President held under the Constitution.
Article 324(1) of the Indian Constitution vests the superintendence, direction, and control of the preparation of electoral rolls and the conduct of all elections to Parliament, State Legislatures, and the offices of the President and Vice-President in the Election Commission of India.
Article 324(2) provides that the Election Commission comprises the Chief Election Commissioner and such number of other Election Commissioners as the President may determine from time to time.
Article 324(3) further stipulates that, when other Election Commissioners are appointed, the Chief Election Commissioner shall serve as the Commission’s Chairman.
For nearly 75 years , Parliament did not enact a law governing the appointment of the CEC and ECs, and the executive made these appointments.
In March 2023 , the Supreme Court ruled against exclusive executive control and provided for a selection committee comprising the Prime Minister, Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha and Chief Justice of India , until Parliament enacted a law.
Parliament subsequently enacted a law in 2023 that excluded the Chief Justice of India and included a Union Cabinet Minister in the three-member selection committee.
The Cabinet Secretary prepares the shortlist , while decisions of the committee are taken by majority vote .
The concern raised is that the presence of the Prime Minister and a Cabinet Minister may give the government a dominant position in the selection process.
The Election Commission exercises significant administrative powers and its decisions directly affect the electoral process and public confidence . The CEC and ECs must therefore be perceived as fair and independent , not merely formally independent.

explain.headline: Industry is growing, but isn’t creating jobs
static: The Periodic Labour Force Survey is regularly conducted by the National Statistical Office to measure employment and unemployment indicators in India.
The Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 regulates labour disputes and requires government permission for lay-offs in industrial establishments employing specified worker counts.
The PM MITRA scheme aims to integrate the textile value chain from spinning to apparel manufacturing in large mega parks to boost exports and employment.
The National Apprenticeship Promotion Scheme provides financial support to employers to engage apprentices and enhance workforce practical skills.
Structural unemployment arises from a mismatch between the skills possessed by the workforce and the skills demanded by available industrial jobs.
explain.what: Formal industrial growth in India is failing to generate sufficient jobs, leaving millions trapped in agriculture or low-paying informal and gig work due to capital-intensive biases and rigid regulations.
explain.why_in_news: The persistent structural challenge of jobless industrial growth and recent data from PLFS 2025 have put employment generation back into policy debates.
explain.background: India faces a structural employment crisis where industrial output expands through capital investments rather than labour absorption, keeping most workers in informal settings.
significance: Highlights the mismatch between industrial growth and actual job creation in the organised sector.
Critiques existing capital-intensive incentive frameworks and rigid labour compliance thresholds.
Provides actionable policy measures like expanding plug-and-play parks and raising lay-off thresholds.
prelims: Nearly 3 in 4 non-farm workers work in informal-sector enterprises according to PLFS 2025.

stories.ai_why: Addresses jobless growth, a key macroeconomic policy challenge.

points: Formal factories are growing steadily, but they remain too small a part of the economy to absorb India's massive workforce.
Invested capital has risen consistently, yet output per worker and wage growth have lagged behind net profits.
Nearly three in four non-farm workers continue to toil in informal-sector enterprises, highlighting a massive formal sector employment shortfall.
Organised manufacturing is dominated by small firms, while factories fail to absorb millions entering the labour force or leaving farming.
Rigid labour rules like the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 threshold push firms to stay small to avoid strict compliance.
Capital-heavy incentives lean towards sectors like semiconductor fabrication plants that create very few jobs per rupee invested.
External shocks such as the 50 percent United States tariff of 2025 on textiles and gems further damage labour-intensive exporters.
The author proposes targeting the Employment Linked Incentive scheme, raising lay-off thresholds, and expanding PM MITRA textile parks.
sum.text:
The takeaway: Formal factories are growing steadily, but they are too small a part of the economy to absorb India’s workers.
Capital over labour: Invested capital has risen steadily, but output per worker has stayed roughly the same over the years.
Profits ahead of wages: Wages per worker have grown more slowly than net profit , so owners gain more from growth than workers do.
Economy-wide effects: Slow wage growth and flat output per worker affect consumption, investment and productivity across the economy.
Informal dominance: Nearly three in four non-farm workers work in informal-sector enterprises , according to the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) 2025 .
Formal shortfall: The formal sector, in both manufacturing and services, simply does not create enough jobs .
Organised versus unorganised: In the previous year, organised manufacturing employed 1.9 crore people against about 3.3 crore in the unorganised segment , according to the Economic Survey .
Firm size matters: Organised manufacturing is dominated by small firms , yet factories with more than 100 workers employ a larger share, pay higher wages and have higher labour productivity .
Missed transition: Factories have not absorbed the millions who enter the labour force each year or who want to leave farming .
Fallback options: Without factory jobs, low-skilled and unskilled workers stay on the farm or take gig work , short platform jobs such as delivery. This is the core of India’s employment challenge .
Size thresholds: Labour rules that tighten above a worker count push firms to stay small . Eg. Lay-off permission above 100 workers under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947.
Capital-heavy incentives: Industrial support often flows to capital-intensive sectors that create few jobs per rupee. Eg. Semiconductor fabrication plants.
Export shocks: Labour-intensive exporters face sudden demand losses. Eg. The 50% United States tariff of 2025 on textiles and gems.
Skill gaps: Many new entrants lack the vocational skills factories need, so firms prefer machines to hiring.
Employment-linked support: The Ministry of Labour and Employment should target the Employment Linked Incentive (ELI) scheme at first-time factory workers.
Higher lay-off threshold: States should apply the Industrial Relations Code, 2020 threshold of 300 workers for lay-off permission, so firms can grow without penalty.
Labour-intensive parks: The Centre should expand PM MITRA textile parks and plug-and-play parks for apparel, leather…

sum.text:
On its part, the ruling dispensation will throw more weight behind Kumar because the INDIA bloc has decided to go all out to target him as part of its 'vote chori' campaign. Kumar is also taking some corrective action, as witnessed, by restoring the original Form 6 in states where the SIR exercise has been completed. However, the Supreme Court will have to specifically weigh in on the manner Form 6 has been used during the SIR.A Supreme Court judge recently stated that the ECI should be manifestly independent.
This can only be achieved if the political class comes to an understanding that the Election Commissioners would not be allowed to enter politics after they demit office. Unfortunately, past experience suggests that this may be impossible to achieve. The Congress not only appointed a CEC who was widely believed to be sympathetic to the party but also made former CEC MS Gill a Rajya Sabha MP as well as a minister.
Was this proper even if no law was transgressed? Should umpires of the electoral process be made players? The ECI's handling of the SIR has been lacking in many respects.
Some corrective action is now being taken to address logical discrepancies and mapping issues. The Commission made onerous demands on many voters, some of which were almost impossible to fulfil. But the real problem is in respect of proving that a person is a citizen if she was born after 1987.
It can be asserted that once the country moved away, in that year, from treating anyone born in India as a citizen, no single document — like a birth certificate — could authoritatively prove a person's citizenship. Indeed, it can equally be asserted that now not even all documents taken together can conclusively prove a person's citizenship if his parents were born after 1987. Ironically, only naturalised citizens have conclusive papers relating to their Indian citizenship.

sum.text:
U S President Donald Trump’s red carpet treatment for his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping during his visit to Washington is more like a return gift for what he received in Beijing earlier this year. Besides the red carpet, Trump welcomed Xi to the White House with a military flyover at Joint Base Andrews along with a display of troops and j ets. Additionally, Trump hosted a grand dinner in the East Room with top technology executives, including Elon Musk, Tim Cook, and Jensen Huang. It was followed by a gift— a three-foot-tall bronze statue of a bald eagle. In May, Xi hosted Trump for bilateral talks at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing, a visit to the Temple of Heaven, and a tour of the Zhongnanhai leadership compound. This marked Trump’s second visit to China and his first during his second term. While Xi lauded the welcome, saying everything during the visit was “done to the highest order of perfection” with “thought in every little detail”, Trump praised the reception as an “epic welcome,” voiced deep appreciation for the hospitality, and commended the personal rapport built with the Chinese President . sum.text:
SpaceX’s Starship, the most powerful launch vehicle ever developed, reached Earth orbit for the first time on Sept. 28, 2026. This mission, the rocket’s 14th test flight, also marked the first time that Starship deployed Starlink internet satellites into the existing larger constellation: 26 new next-generation nodes in total.
But not all went as planned. An engine went out, though SpaceX quickly determined Starship could still reach orbit without it. While SpaceX had planned for Starship to orbit the Earth six times, it changed gears and had Starship return after only two orbits. And the splashdown in the Pacific Ocean ended in a huge bang, rather than the soft landing the company had hoped for.
This flight can still be viewed as a success. It was an important step toward putting the enormous rocket to work by sending it into orbit. Starship is a key part of SpaceX’s vision. The company wants Starship to be a fully and rapidly reusable transport system that slashes the cost of spaceflight.
To realize this vision of extremely low-cost launches , SpaceX needs to be able to bring these spacecraft back from orbit, refurbish them and launch them again in short order.
Whether that all becomes quick and routine largely depends on dark ceramic tiles covering Starship’s underside. These tiles make up Starship’s heat shield .
I’m an engineer and professor who has researched the way heat shields respond when reentering the atmosphere , a process that is extremely harsh on a spacecraft. I see Starship’s heat shield as a technical challenge that also drives the company’s economics. Elon Musk has agreed .
A spacecraft that survives its return has passed an essential test. Next, engineers must establish how much work it will take to repair or replace the heat shield before its next launch.
A spacecraft in low Earth orbit travels at roughly 17,500 miles per hour (28,000 kilometers per hour). Returning to Earth means shedding an enormous amount of energy to slow down. Some shedding happens higher up by igniting the engine, but a lot of it happens lower down as the spacecraft reenters through the atmosphere . During reentry, strong shock waves form and heat up the surrounding atmosphere. Much of that heat transfers to the spacecraft.

sum.text: The EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) represents a fundamental change in the way international trade will increasingly be conducted. What began as an environmental measure is becoming an important determinant of market access and competitiveness. Indian exporters should not view it merely as another European compliance requirement, but as an early indication of how carbon intensity will influence global trade over the coming decade. The definitive phase of EU CBAM commenced on January 1. It covers 6 carbon-intensive sectors - iron and steel, aluminium, cement, fertilisers, electricity, and hydrogen. EU importers above the prescribed threshold must account for embedded emissions and surrender CBAM certificates linked to the EU Emissions Trading System carbon price. Importantly, a carbon price effectively paid in the country of production can be deducted from the CBAM liability. For India, the immediate exposure is relevant to iron and steel and aluminium. But we shouldn't look at CBAM only through the prism of its coverage. The direction of travel is much wider. The EU is moving towards extending CBAM to selected downstream products containing substantial quantities of iron, steel and aluminium, while further examination of additional sectors, indirect emissions and downstream products is envisaged. Organic chemicals and polymers have also figured in the review framework. Thus, engineering goods, fabricated metal products and, eventually, several products further down manufacturing value chains could face increasing carbon-related compliance. The issue is consequently much larger than exports presently falling under CBAM. India must prepare for this transition now, particularly keeping MSMEs at the centre of its response. Large companies have greater capacity to measure emissions, engage accredited verifiers, procure RE and invest in cleaner tech. For a small exporter, however, measurement, reporting, verification and certification can become significant costs even before any carbon levy is imposed. International practice also recognises need for proportionality. The EU has introduced a 50-tonne threshold that exempts many smaller importers while retaining more than 99% of emissions within CBAM. The UK CBAM, scheduled from 2027, provides a registration threshold intended to reduce disproportionate administrative burdens on smaller businesses. India should follow the same principle while supporting its exporters. GoI has moved in the right…

sum.text:
The Goondas Act has been invoked against Gem Granites Owner R Veeramani and two others- Shanthi and Mahendra Simhan- who were arrested in connection with a POCSO case, police said on Thursday. The preventive detention orders against the three were issued by the Chennai City Police Commissioner.
Veeramani, Shanthi and Mahendra Simhan were arrested following allegations of sexual offences against minors. The case was subsequently taken up for investigation by a Special Investigation Team (SIT) constituted by the Tamil Nadu Police.
The SIT has been probing the allegations against the accused and has also been examining complaints received in connection with the case. The three accused are currently in judicial custody, and further investigation is underway.
The case relates to allegations of sexual assault involving minor girls. Police had initially registered the case after receiving a USB drive containing a video allegedly showing a minor girl being sexually assaulted at a guest house in Teynampet.
The accused businessman was arrested on August 29 along with two other alleged accused. A POCSO Special Court subsequently granted three days of custody for his interrogation. Considering his age and health, the questioning was conducted inside Puzhal prison under video recording by the Central Crime Branch's Anti-Vice Squad.
Police later identified seven additional minor girls allegedly linked to the case, and their statements were recorded before the Special Court dealing with POCSO cases. After one survivor was found to belong to a Scheduled Caste community, provisions of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act were also added to the case.
The Tamil Nadu government has directed police to intensify the investigation and identify and take action against everyone found to be connected with the alleged offences. A special team comprising women police Sub-Inspectors has also been formed to identify minor girls appearing in the video and assist in the ongoing probe.
The Central Crime Branch is now examining the earlier investigation and the circumstances surrounding the closure of the case. (ANI)

The High Court also upheld life imprisonment for 11 other convicts, saying their roles in terror training camps in Gujarat and Keralam, and logistical support to the conspiracy, had been proved.

On July 26, 2008, a series of 21 bomb blasts hit different parts of Ahmedabad within 70 minutes, killing 56 people and injuring more than 200 others. sum.text:
On Gandhi Jayanti, Mahatma Gandhi’s familiar face will be everywhere — in tributes, photographs and remembrances marking his birth anniversary. But there is one place where his portrait is already an everyday presence: the Indian rupee.
Gandhi’s portrait is now so closely associated with Indian currency that a banknote without his familiar face can seem difficult to imagine. Yet, when independent India began deciding what its new currency should look like, Gandhi was not the choice that ultimately made it to the country’s first redesigned banknotes.
So, on Gandhi Jayanti , here’s the story of how a portrait that did not make the cut for independent India’s first banknotes eventually became the enduring face of the Indian rupee.
India became independent on August 15, 1947, but its currency did not change overnight. During the transition, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) continued to issue existing notes carrying the portrait of King George VI.
As India began looking for a replacement for the colonial imagery, Gandhi’s portrait was initially considered and designs were prepared. But the idea did not make the final cut.
“In the final analysis, the consensus moved to the choice of the Lion Capital at Sarnath in lieu of the Gandhi Portrait,” the RBI says.
In 1949, the Government of India introduced a new Re 1 note with the Lion Capital of Ashoka at Sarnath in the watermark window. Independent India’s first new banknote had arrived — without Gandhi.
For the next several decades, India’s banknotes featured a range of symbols and themes rather than being centred around one individual.
The designs reflected India’s wildlife, art, agriculture, infrastructure and scientific progress. Different notes over the years carried imagery such as deer and peacocks, the Konark Wheel, agricultural activity and the Hirakud Dam.
By the 1980s, the themes had expanded further. The Aryabhatta satellite represented India’s advances in science and technology, while other notes depicted oil rigs and farm mechanisation.
Indian currency during these decades, therefore, used different denominations to showcase aspects of the country’s heritage and development.

For exporters, the immediate impact is continuity rather than a new benefit: eligible shipments can continue to receive RoDTEP support under the applicable rules during the extended period.

President Droupadi Murmu has given her assent to the Gujarat Uniform Civil Code (UCC) Bill, 2026, making it the second state in independent India after Uttarakhand to codify a common set of personal laws. The state government will notify the rules for the code, after which the law will come into force. The legislation, passed after an eight-hour debate on March 24, exempts the state’s Scheduled Tribe (ST) population.
Chief minister Bhupendra Patel tabled it a week after a panel headed by retired Supreme Court judge Justice Ranjana Prakash Desai submitted its report. Justice Desai had previously headed the committee that drafted the Uttarakhand code. Moving the Bill, Patel had said, “This Bill has been introduced for the sisters and daughters of Gujarat.
The state has taken a step towards accelerating the pace of a developed India by 2047 through the UCC. This Bill ensures that no community is discriminated against. It does not take away anyone’s rights or restrict anyone’s freedom.” He added that the objective was social harmony and national unity, and noted that the Supreme Court had suggested a uniform code to secure women’s rights.
“It is our responsibility to safeguard the rights and dignity of daughters. In this Bill, respect for women is there. It is a matter of women’s empowerment,” he told the House.
Both Congress and the Aam Aadmi Party had requested that the Bill be referred to a select committee, while Opposition members termed the legislation anti-Muslim and alleged it was being brought for political gain — a charge the government rejected. The UCC is the third of the three core agendas the ruling BJP has championed since its inception, the other two being the construction of the Ram temple in Ayodhya and the scrapping of Article 370, which gave special status to Jammu and Kashmir. With this, Gujarat has become the second state, after Uttarakhand, to enact a comprehensive UCC — a common set of laws governing marriage, divorce and inheritance.
Assam and Madhya Pradesh — both BJP-ruled states — have also passed UCC legislation, but neither has been implemented yet. Maharashtra, Chhattisgarh and Rajasthan — also governed by the BJP — have set up drafting committees to introduce a UCC Bill. sum.text:
Canada and India are aiming to scale their bilateral trade from USD 30 billion to USD 70 billion over the next five years, with ongoing free trade negotiations expected to conclude in the coming months, Canadian International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu said on Thursday (local time).
Speaking at the 2026 G20 Trade Ministers Meeting in Milwaukee on the India-Canada trade deal, Sidhu said, "The vision that leaders have set out for us is to scale trade from USD 30 billion to USD 70 billion within the next five years. How do we get there? Part of it is through the greater facilitation of free trade. Right now, negotiations are ongoing to see what we can do together to build our economies in a complementary manner rather than competing with one another."
Highlighting the recent momentum in talks, the Canadian minister noted that the fifth round of negotiations for the trade agreement is scheduled to take place in Ottawa on Monday. "I was just in India about 10 days ago, meeting with Minister Piyush Goyal in Mumbai. We were discussing Round 4 then. Round 5 will happen in Ottawa on Monday, and we are going to continue those conversations. Of course, negotiations are always tough, but we look forward to concluding in the coming months. It is important that Canada continues to have these conversations. Prime Minister Carney and Prime Minister Modi have had excellent conversations on how we can bring our economies closer together,’ Sidhu said.
Underlining Canada's existing financial footprint in India, Sidhu pointed out that “Canada is the largest collective investor in India, with over USD 100 billion invested. Canadian companies are involved in many infrastructure projects there, building airports and highways. We want to see more cooperation, and we also welcome Indian investors to invest in our mining and energy projects so we can grow together. It involves trade, investments, research, and collaboration."
Sidhu emphasised that energy and critical minerals form the cornerstone of the strategic economic alignment between the two nations, noting, “India's economy is growing at 7% year-over-year, and the country will require 70% more energy by 2035. We have that energy in Canada. Prime Minister Carney just launched the LNG Canada Phase 2 two days ago, which is going to be the second-largest LNG project in the world... As India builds, Canada wants to be there to help build India as well.”

Scientists at the CSIR-Centre for Cellular and Molecular Biology (CCMB) developed an India-specific disease severity score for sickle cell anaemia on 2 October 2026. The tool was built from clinical data of 171 Indian children aged up to 18 years treated at the Government Medical College and Hospital, Nagpur.
Sickle cell anaemia is an inherited blood disorder caused by abnormal haemoglobin, and it is classified as a haemoglobinopathy. The disease can produce anaemia, pain episodes, and organ-related complications, and its clinical pattern varies across populations.
The revised model is named ISS1, which stands for India-specific Severity Score. ISS1 improved clinical assessment accuracy to nearly 83 per cent, while ISS2 used observable clinical indicators instead of laboratory measurements and achieved about 85 per cent concordance.
ISS2 correctly identified all patients in the mild category. The design of ISS2 allows clinicians to make management decisions without extensive laboratory investigations.
The Paediatric Severity Score, or PSS, is a widely used international scoring system based on patient data from outside India. In the Indian study, PSS matched expert clinical assessments in about 67 per cent of cases.

Nehru reportedly dismissed this suggestion, missing India's chance for permanent membership. Currently, there is no clear timeline for when, or if, India will achieve this goal. India believes the current UNSC structure no longer reflects modern realities. It argues that its status as the largest democracy and its growing economy make it a key global player. India's commitment to peace is shown through its significant involvement in UN peacekeeping missions, where it has sent many personnel to help maintain stability. sum.text:
India and Japan on Thursday unveiled an ambitious roadmap to further strengthen their Special Strategic and Global Partnership, with Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi agreeing to deepen cooperation in defence, economic security, artificial intelligence (AI), clean energy, high-speed rail, resilient supply chains and people-to-people exchanges.
Following the 16th India-Japan Annual Summit in New Delhi, the two leaders reaffirmed their commitment to advancing bilateral ties based on three priority pillars — defence and security cooperation; economic partnership, including economic security, energy resilience, technology and innovation; and stronger people-to-people exchanges. They said a stronger India-Japan partnership would contribute to a free, open, resilient and prosperous Indo-Pacific amid an increasingly uncertain global geopolitical environment.

explain.headline: Wayanad vulture survey records 65 birds in Keralam
static: Vultures are vital scavenging birds of prey that play a crucial role in maintaining ecosystem health by disposing of animal carcasses.
India hosts several vulture species, notably the White-rumped Vulture, Indian Vulture, Slender-billed Vulture, and Red-headed Vulture.
Diclofenac, a veterinary non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug, historically caused catastrophic declines in Indian vulture populations through kidney failure.
Conservation breeding programmes and a ban on the veterinary use of diclofenac have been key regulatory steps taken in India.
Protected areas like wildlife sanctuaries and national parks provide essential safe habitats and food sources for surviving vulture populations.

points: A two-day vulture survey in the Wayanad Wildlife Sanctuary recorded a total of 65 individual birds.
The recorded population comprises 54 White-rumped Vultures and 11 Red-headed Vultures.
The survey highlights Wayanad's continued significance as Keralam's only known vulture habitat.
The exercise was jointly conducted by the Forest Department, Wayanad Wildlife Division, WWF-India, and the Hume Centre for Ecology and Wildlife Biology.
Forty-two participants including birdwatchers, researchers, and students operated across nine observation points in four forest ranges.
Teams made 108 total observations totaling 243 sightings, which were filtered by timing, distance, and flight direction to yield the 65 unique count.
Favourable habitat conditions include connectivity with large forests and food availability from large mammal carcasses.

sum.text:
Wayanad (Keralam), Oct 1 (PTI) A two-day survey in the Wayanad Wildlife Sanctuary has recorded 65 vultures, comprising 54 White-rumped and 11 Red-headed Vultures, underscoring Wayanad's significance as Keralam's only vulture habitat.
In the forested hills of Wayanad, vultures can often be seen soaring above the trees, riding warm air currents.
According to a release, the survey provided a clearer picture of the presence and distribution of vultures in the region.
The survey was jointly conducted by the Forest Department, Wayanad Wildlife Division, WWF-India and the Hume Centre for Ecology and Wildlife Biology.
Forty-two birdwatchers, researchers, students and wildlife enthusiasts from different parts of Keralam took part in the survey. They worked in nine groups at observation points across the sanctuary.
Seven observation points were selected across the sanctuary's four forest ranges—Edakombam and Nallathanni in the Bathery Range; Kakkapadam and Marathakam in the Muthanga Range; Doddakkulashi in the Kurichiad Range; and Punchavayal and Ayyappanpara in the Tholpetty Range.
The locations were chosen to represent different parts of the sanctuary, with priority given to high vantage points offering unobstructed views. From these locations, vultures flying high in the sky or circling overhead could be spotted more easily, the release said.
Over the two days, the teams made 108 observations and recorded 243 vultures. However, the figure did not represent 243 individual birds, as the same bird could have been sighted from more than one observation point.
Vultures travel across large areas, and researchers therefore examined the timing of each sighting, the distance from the observation point, the direction of flight and movement patterns before assessing the records.
The analysis brought the number of individual vultures recorded during the survey period to 65.
The findings underline the importance of Wayanad as a habitat for vultures in Keralam.
The sanctuary's connectivity with large stretches of forest and the availability of food, including carcasses of large mammals, provide favourable conditions for these scavenging birds, the release said. However, determining the number of vultures present is only the first step.
Continuous monitoring is needed to understand changes in their population and movement patterns, as well as threats such as poisoning and electrocution, the researchers said. PTI TGB SSK

sum.text:
New Delhi: More than 2.42 lakh special gram sabhas were held across the country to discuss transformative governance reforms on Gandhi Jayanti, marking the Centre’s launch of the People’s Plan Campaign 2026-27 under which Gram Panchayats will prepare their development plans for the next financial year. The gram sabhas held on Friday -- with participation from locals, elected representatives, Panchayat functionaries and officials -- placed various government schemes and local issues at the centre of discussions, the Ministry of Panchayati Raj said in a statement. The special gram sabhas provided rural citizens a “direct platform” to participate in discussions on key government initiatives and issues of local relevance, it said.
The deliberations covered the devolution of Central Finance Commission grants to panchayats, financial self-reliance through own-source revenue, property and land rights, employment and livelihoods, drinking water and sanitation, water security, food security, consumer protection and women’s economic empowerment. Agenda and information on key government initiatives, including governance reforms and citizen-centric measures undertaken over the last 12 years, were read out and discussed. Participants shared their experiences and suggestions, the ministry said.
The exercise was supported by various ministries and departments as well as their field-level functionaries and MY Bharat volunteers. Their engagement at the state-, district-, block- and gram panchayat-level helped facilitate meaningful dialogue on citizen-centric schemes and initiatives while strengthening “Jan Bhagidari and Samvaad at the grassroots”, it said. Panchayati Raj Secretary Vineet Joshi and senior officials of the ministry and participating departments were in touch with officials of states and Union Territories throughout the day to review the progress of the gram sabhas and facilitate coordination, the statement said.
The special gram sabhas also marked the commencement of the People’s Plan Campaign 2026-27, “Sabki Yojana, Sabka Vikas”, under which panchayats will prepare their development plans for the financial year 2027-28. The campaign, led by the Ministry of Panchayati Raj in collaboration with 21 ministries and departments, has been rolled out across all states and Union Territories since 2018 to enable panchayats to prepare evidence-based, holistic and participatory plans.

sum.text:
CHENNAI: Chief Minister C Joseph Vijay on Friday launched the expanded Vettri Payanam scheme at the Koyambedu bus terminus, under which women and transgender persons can travel free of cost in government buses across Tamil Nadu. Vijay formally launched the scheme by distributing free tickets to women passengers waiting inside buses at the terminus. The gesture marked the commencement of the expanded free-travel facility, which is expected to benefit around 84.32 lakh women every day.
A total of 12,692 government buses have been brought under the expanded scheme. This accounts for 69% of the 18,413 scheduled buses operated by the seven state transport undertakings. Of the total 1,94,649 scheduled trips (singles), 1,65,312 trips, or 85%, will be operated under the scheme.
The expansion covers Express, LSS and Deluxe buses operating within cities and urban areas, Mofussil Ordinary buses and Ghat Ordinary buses operating beyond 40 km, in addition to the services already covered by the free-travel scheme. However, buses operated by State Express Transport Corporation (SETC) have been excluded from the scheme..The implementation of this scheme will entail an annual expenditure of approximately Rs 6,000 crore. Under the women’s free bus travel scheme (Vidiyal Payanam) launched by previous DMK government, women are permitted to travel only in ordinary city and town buses and ordinary buses operating in hilly areas for distances up to 40 km.
Free travel was not permitted in Express, LSS, Deluxe and Mofussil buses. The Electronic Ticketing Machine (ETM) systems in the buses have been integrated to record the free journeys. The government had completed the integration work, with testing and verification and trial runs were conducted on September 27.

sum.text:
A penguin that looked like all the others has turned out to be something quite different. Scientists have identified the southeastern gentoo as a new species after discovering genetic differences that had gone unnoticed for more than 100 years.
Penguins may seem like one of the easier animals to identify. They have their familiar black-and-white feathers, waddling walk and flipper-like wings. But scientists have discovered that even penguins can keep a few secrets.
Researchers have identified a new species of penguin for the first time in more than 100 years, and the biggest clue was not a striking change in appearance. It was hidden inside the birds' DNA.
The newly recognised species is called the southeastern gentoo penguin, or Pygoscelis kerguelensis. It lives on the remote Kerguelen Islands in the southern Indian Ocean, about 1,200 miles north of Antarctica.
The discovery means that what scientists had long considered one gentoo penguin species is actually four distinct species.
An international team of 22 researchers analysed the genomes of 64 gentoo penguins from 10 breeding colonies, covering almost the entire known range of the birds.
Their analysis revealed four genetically distinct lineages: the northern gentoo (Pygoscelis papua), southern gentoo (Pygoscelis ellsworthi), eastern gentoo (Pygoscelis taeniata) and the newly recognised southeastern gentoo (Pygoscelis kerguelensis).
The four groups appear to have separated from one another roughly 300,000 to 500,000 years ago. Geographic isolation and differences between their environments are thought to have helped drive that evolution.
The southeastern gentoo is particularly interesting because it is what scientists call a cryptic species. In simple terms, it looks so similar to a closely related species that its separate identity is difficult to spot just by looking at it.
Researchers found some subtle differences in characteristics such as size and vocalisations, but the genetic differences were much clearer.
Perhaps the most surprising part of the discovery is that the new species was not recently found by someone exploring an unknown island.
Scientists had actually collected a specimen of the southeastern gentoo on Kerguelen Island in 1897.
For more than a century, the penguins from the islands were grouped with other gentoo populations because their physical appearance was so similar. It was only with modern genomic analysis that researchers could establish that they represented a separate…

sum.text:
New Delhi: India and the Netherlands have agreed to strengthen their agricultural partnership by expanding cooperation in areas such as agricultural innovation, horticulture and the seed sector, Union Agriculture and Farmers Welfare Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan said following bilateral discussions with Dutch Agriculture Minister Silvio Erkens, the Ministry of Agriculture & Farmers Welfare said on Friday. The meeting reviewed ongoing collaboration between the two countries and explored new avenues for cooperation aimed at enhancing farm productivity through technology, innovation and knowledge sharing. During the discussions, both sides assessed the progress of the 25 Centres of Excellence (CoEs) established in the agriculture and horticulture sectors under the India-Netherlands partnership.
The Centres of Excellence have been playing a key role in promoting modern farming techniques, protected cultivation and advanced horticultural practices across several Indian states. Chouhan and Erkens also agreed to examine opportunities for cooperation in the seed sector through the formulation of a dedicated work plan. The proposed framework is expected to identify priority areas and provide a roadmap for effective implementation of joint initiatives.
Agricultural innovation emerged as another major focus area during the talks. Both countries discussed potential areas of collaboration, acknowledging the significant advancements made by India and the Netherlands in agricultural research, technology adoption and innovation-driven farming practices. The meeting underscored the shared commitment of both nations to promoting sustainable and technology-led agricultural growth while facilitating the exchange of expertise and best practices.
The Dutch delegation was led by Silvio Erkens, Minister for Agriculture, Fisheries, Food Security and Nature, and included Director General Marten van den Berg, Netherlands Ambassador to India Marisa Gerards and other senior officials. sum.text:
Jawahar Dweep Marine Oil Terminal in Mumbai was declared plastic-free on 2 October 2026 by the Mumbai Port Authority. The terminal became India’s first oil terminal to eliminate single-use plastics completely.
Jawahar Dweep is also known as Butcher Island and is an offshore facility located about four kilometres off Mumbai’s coast. It has five jetties and handles crude oil and petroleum products.
The terminal serves major refineries such as Bharat Petroleum Corporation Limited, Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited, Indian Oil Corporation Limited, and Oil and Natural Gas Corporation. Petroleum cargo accounts for nearly three-fifths of Mumbai Port’s total traffic.
The plastic-free declaration was made during Swachhata Abhiyan 2026 at Grey Gate in Indira Dock. The programme was held on 2 October, the birth anniversary of Mahatma Gandhi .
The Mumbai Port Authority has planned reductions in single-use plastics across its docks, residential colonies, and coastal areas. The initiative covers operational and residential spaces under the port administration.
Union Minister for Ports, Shipping and Waterways Sarbananda Sonowal dedicated the port’s new Oil Spill Response facilities to the nation on 2 October 2026. Oil Spill Response systems are used for containment, recovery, and control of marine oil pollution.

The audit covering 2019-20 to 2023-24 highlighted that the institutional implementation mechanism in J&K was neither fully operational nor effective.
Issues included shortfalls in District Water Sanitation Mission meetings, absence of a bottom-up approach, and failure to prepare district annual action plans.
Target achievements for functional household tap connections showed shortfalls ranging from 6 per cent to 93 per cent across state action plans.
By March 31, 2024, out of total rural households, 14,43,515 representing 77.15 per cent were reported to have been provided with tap connections.
Only 44 per cent of schemes taken up between 2019-20 and 2023-24 under the programme were completed as of December 2024.
Support activities and Water Quality Monitoring and Surveillance components saw severe under-utilisation, falling short of their prescribed spending ceilings.
Sampled districts like Kulgam, Anantnag, Kishtwar, and Doda showed poor physical completion rates alongside an absence of operation and maintenance plans.

sum.text:
The Government of Jammu and Kashmir was not able to receive full central assistance allocated under the Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM) due to delays in utilisation of funds and failure to meet the conditions required for release of funds, a report of Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) has observed. The flagship JJM scheme was launched on August 15, 2019, with the aim of providing functional household tap connection (FHTC) to every rural household. The performance audit of the scheme covering the period from 2019-20 to 2023-24 revealed that the institutional mechanism for successful implementation of the programme was not fully operational and effective in J&K. There were shortfalls in holding the prescribed number of meetings of the District Water Sanitation Mission, a lack of bottom-up approach in the preparation of action plans and non-preparation of district annual action plans.“The accumulation of idle balances, delayed execution of schemes and delayed access of potable water to rural households were also seen.
Due to delay in utilisation of funds and inability to meet release conditions, the Government of Jammu & Kashmir could not receive the full allocation of central assistance,” the CAG report stated. The audit found that there was a shortfall ranging from 6 per cent to 93 per cent in the achievement of targets for FHTCs fixed under state action plans. As of 31 March 2024, 14,43,515 (77.15 per cent) households were reported to have been provided with FHTCs.
Despite sizeable allocations of funds, persistent underutilisation of funds during the initial years was observed. Only 44 per cent schemes (1,440 out of 3,253 total schemes) taken up during 2019-20 to 2023-24 under the programme were completed as of December 2024.“The release of funds for support activities ranged from 0.17 per cent to 3.3 per cent, falling short of the prescribed ceiling of 5 per cent. While under Water Quality Monitoring and Surveillance (WQM&S) activities, it ranged from 0.08 per cent to 1.07 per cent, against the provision of 2 per cent.
The non-adherence to prescribed funding allocations and poor utilisation under support and WQM&S components indicated inadequate emphasis after 2021-22 on critical activities like water quality surveillance, community awareness and institutional capacity building,” the audit stated. sum.text:
Prayagraj: Products from small towns of Uttar Pradesh are increasingly finding a place in international markets, and Fatehpur’s famed Malwan peda has now joined the list. A local trader has secured an export order from Italy after showcasing the traditional sweet at the recently concluded UP International Trade Show under the One District One Product (ODOP) scheme. Sohanlal Gupta, proprietor of Malwan ka Sohan Peda, said the trade show delivered what generations of his family had only dreamt of.
He received an order to supply 200 kg of peda to an Italian company, Domenico Percoco. Domenico Percoco is a renowned Italian food joint, celebrated primarily for its traditional flavours and cuisine. It is also popular for serving Italian-style pizzas, sandwiches, fries and other snacks.
The development marks a significant milestone for the sweet, which is among Uttar Pradesh’s many distinctive regional varieties of peda that enjoy popularity among food enthusiasts for their unique flavours and preparation methods. Historian and former Allahabad University faculty member Dr Heramb Chaturvedi said the origins of peda are widely associated with Mathura, where condensed milk solids, or mawa, have traditionally been offered to Lord Krishna. Before refrigeration became commonplace, surplus milk was slow-cooked for hours to produce khoya or mawa, preventing spoilage.
Sugar and cardamom were then mixed into the thickened milk to create the flattened sweet known as peda. The story of Malwan peda dates back to the 1960s. According to local accounts, Mohanlal Gupta, who ran a tea stall in Malwan, began making peda from surplus milk left over after preparing tea.
Over time, the sweet gained popularity and evolved into three prominent brands: Mohan Peda, Sohan Peda and Mahesh (Ganesh) Peda. Gupta said Malwan peda is known for its purity, distinctive earthy aroma and rich taste. Unlike conventional pedas made from prepared mawa, sugar is added directly to raw milk sourced from local dairy farmers.
The milk is simmered for hours until it develops its characteristic flavour, after which green cardamom is added. Sugar is used sparingly to preserve the sweet’s natural aroma. The pedas are also significantly larger than standard varieties.

sum.text:
Bangladesh Foreign Minister Dr. Khalilur Rahman was elected President of the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) on Tuesday, defeating Cypriot diplomat Andreas Kakouris in a closely contested vote.
Rahman secured 99 votes against Kakouris’ 91 in the election held among the 193-member UN body. He will assume office in September when the 81st session of the General Assembly begins, succeeding current President Annalena Baerbock.
Following his election, External Affairs Minister Dr. S. Jaishankar said in a post on X, “Congratulations to FM Dr. Khalilur Rahman of Bangladesh on his election as President of the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly. Look forward to working closely with him to advance our shared priorities and strengthen multilateral cooperation.”
India’s Permanent Representative to the United Nations, Parvathaneni Harish, also extended his congratulations, reaffirming India’s commitment to multilateralism and the United Nations.
Rahman, who became Bangladesh’s Foreign Minister in February, is a career diplomat with extensive experience in international affairs. He has previously served at Bangladesh’s Permanent Mission to the United Nations, worked within the UN system, and held the position of National Security Adviser.
Addressing the General Assembly after his election, Rahman announced the theme of his presidency as “Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations that Delivers for All.”
“The eighty-first session of the Assembly will open at a historic crossroads,” Rahman said, highlighting the challenges facing the international community, including global conflicts, economic uncertainties, and sustainable development concerns.
He pledged to work with member states to prevent “another lost decade” of development and stressed the importance of multilateral cooperation in addressing global crises. Drawing on Bangladesh’s longstanding contribution to UN peacekeeping operations, Rahman said his country’s experience would help guide efforts to build consensus and strengthen international cooperation.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres welcomed Rahman’s election, saying the United Nations would benefit greatly from his “remarkable political and diplomatic experience.” He noted that Rahman would assume leadership of the Assembly at a time of both significant challenges and important opportunities for the organisation.
